entries.term: Minor versions kept in standard support
Extended / long-term support past standard window
The most recent Kubernetes minor release generally available on the service as of the May 2026 snapshot.
How many Kubernetes minor versions are concurrently offered under the service's standard (non-extended) support window.
Ability to keep a cluster on a Kubernetes minor version after standard support ends — usually at an additional cost.
The financially-backed monthly uptime percentage the provider commits to for the Kubernetes API server / control plane.
What the provider charges per cluster for the managed control plane itself, separate from worker-node compute.
Run worker nodes on discounted, interruptible capacity for fault-tolerant or batch workloads.
Provision worker nodes with attached GPUs for ML training, inference and other accelerated workloads.
Run worker nodes on ARM-architecture CPUs, typically for better price-performance.
Automatically grow and shrink node pools to fit pending pod demand, using the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler or an equivalent.
A Karpenter-class provisioner that launches right-sized nodes per pending pod, instead of scaling pre-defined, fixed-instance-type node pools.
Whether the autoscaling layer itself provisions interruptible Spot capacity and handles interruptions — beyond a hand-created static Spot node pool.
Whether an autoscaling node pool can scale all the way down to zero nodes when there is no demand.
Whether the platform actively repacks workloads onto fewer or cheaper nodes and removes under-utilised — not just empty — nodes.
The largest node count the provider documents or recommends for a single cluster (default quota, before special increases).
The container-network-interface plugin the service installs by default for pod networking.
Whether the service lets you swap in a different CNI (e.g. Cilium) or run it bring-your-own.
Named tracks (rapid / regular / stable) that govern which Kubernetes versions a cluster is offered and how quickly.
Whether the provider can automatically upgrade the control plane and worker nodes to newer Kubernetes versions.
Long-lived static keys (and how to avoid them)
Permissions attached to a principal (user, group, role, service identity) that say what that principal may do.
A policy attached to the resource itself, naming who may access it — enables cross-account / cross-tenant grants without touching the caller's identity.
What you actually author — JSON, a DSL, a portal abstraction. Determines how readable, diffable and version-controllable your access config is.
Curated permission sets maintained by the provider, so you are not assembling every permission by hand.
With no matching grant, the request is denied. The universal baseline of least privilege.
The ability to write a rule that forbids an action — and have it beat any allow. The cornerstone of guardrails.
When an allow and a deny both match, which wins. Determines whether guardrails are actually enforceable.
An upper bound on what a principal can ever be granted — the effective permissions are the intersection of the grant and the ceiling.
A tree of accounts/projects/subscriptions above the individual workload, for blast-radius isolation and delegated administration.
A grant or restriction made high in the hierarchy automatically applying to everything beneath it.
Whether human and app identities live in a dedicated identity service separate from the resource-permission layer.
Letting an external workload (CI runner, another cloud, an OIDC IdP) exchange its own token for cloud credentials — no stored secret.
A VM / container / function receiving an identity automatically, so application code calls cloud APIs with no credential to store.
Per-pod cloud identity in managed Kubernetes, so each workload gets least-privilege access without sharing the node's identity.
Federating an enterprise SAML IdP so workforce users sign in to the cloud without separate cloud credentials.
Time-boxed credentials that expire on their own — the alternative to long-lived static keys.
Whether permanent access keys exist at all — and whether the provider gives you a clean keyless path so you never need them.
How one of the provider's own services is authorised to call another on your behalf.
Refining a grant with conditions on the request — source IP, time, MFA, transport, tags.
Authorising on the attributes of the principal and the resource (e.g. matching tags) rather than enumerating identities — access that scales without editing policy.
Membership of a group defined by a rule over attributes, rather than an explicit member list — so identities join and leave automatically.
Service-to-service token issuance via client_id / client_secret. Table stakes for B2B APIs.
User-facing flow with PKCE for SPAs and mobile. The expected default for public clients in 2026.
Validate signed JWTs against a JWKS endpoint, with claim extraction for downstream routing/auth.
Verify client certificates at the gateway. Increasingly required for B2B and zero-trust setups.
Simple shared-secret identification (not authentication). Still common for partner-tier consumption.
Delegate authz decisions to an external policy engine — OPA, custom service, etc.
Throttle requests at the API level — protect backends from sudden spikes.
Different quotas for different consumers (free tier vs pro vs enterprise).
Stop hitting an unhealthy backend before it cascades. Often paired with retries + timeouts.
Retry idempotent calls with exponential backoff. Hide transient backend hiccups.
The longest the gateway waits for the upstream backend to respond before it gives up.
The largest request body the gateway will accept — a hard wall on file uploads and bulk calls.
Whether the gateway imposes an out-of-the-box request-rate ceiling before you configure any policy.
How the gateway enforces longer-window consumption quotas — per day, week or month.
Modify headers, body, query strings on the way through. The classic gateway job.
Proxy GraphQL queries without inspection. Minimum baseline for GraphQL APIs.
Compose multiple REST/gRPC backends into a single GraphQL schema at the gateway.
Proxy gRPC or transcode HTTP/JSON ↔ gRPC. Important for internal services.
Export traces in OTel format. Required for modern observability stacks.
Out-of-the-box dashboards for API traffic, latency, errors. No-setup observability.
Track who changed what in the API config — required for many compliance regimes.
Run the gateway in your own infrastructure (not just SaaS). Often required for regulated industries.
Declarative config via CRDs. Integrates cleanly with ArgoCD / Flux.
Run the same APIs across multiple regions with automatic routing / failover.
Route N% of traffic to a new version. Crucial for safe rollouts.
Customer-facing portal for API discovery, key request, docs. Marketing surface for API products.
Bootstrap an API from an OpenAPI spec. Quality varies — round-tripping is the real test.
Can you actually ship a small product without paying? Some vendors say 'free' but limit so harshly it's effectively a trial.
Apache 2 / MIT / similar permissive license, with a viable production path on the OSS edition alone.
Linear scaling with traffic (rather than seats / instances / enterprise contracts).
Required for US federal agency workloads. Lengthy authorization process — vendors that have it have it.
BAA available; can be used for PHI workloads. Healthcare and adjacent industries.
Annual SOC 2 attestation. Table stakes for most B2B SaaS sales.

FedRAMP authorizes cloud services for use by US federal agencies. Authorizations are issued at an impact level — Low, Moderate or High — and are scoped to a specific named environment and a defined in-scope service list. The level is the headline; the region is the fine print.

The US Department of Defense layers its own Cloud Computing SRG impact levels (IL2, IL4, IL5, IL6) on top of FedRAMP. IL4/IL5 cover Controlled Unclassified Information and require a DISA Provisional Authorization, typically in dedicated government regions.

The Australian Information Security Registered Assessors Program (IRAP) provides an independent assessment of a cloud service against the Australian Government's Information Security Manual (ISM). It is an assessment, not a government certification — agencies make their own risk decision against it.

The Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue (C5) is issued by Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI). Providers obtain a C5 attestation from an independent auditor (an ISAE 3000-style report), widely expected by German public sector and regulated buyers.

The Esquema Nacional de Seguridad (ENS) is Spain's National Security Framework, mandatory for public-sector systems. Cloud providers obtain ENS certification at a category — Basic, Medium or High — from an accredited certification body.

ISO/IEC 27001 certifies an Information Security Management System (ISMS) against an international standard. The certificate has a Statement of Applicability that defines which services, locations and data centres are in scope — the scope statement is the substance.

A SOC 2 report is an independent auditor's attestation against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, confidentiality, etc.). SOC 2 reports are confidential and obtained under NDA — the provider does not publish the report itself, only the fact that it exists.

PCI DSS is the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard. A cloud provider can be certified as a compliant service provider — but PCI scope is a shared-responsibility split: the provider's Attestation of Compliance (AOC) covers in-scope services only, and the customer's own environment must still be assessed.

HIPAA is US health-data regulation. There is no government 'HIPAA certification' for a cloud — instead a provider signs a Business Associate Addendum (BAA) and designates which services are 'HIPAA-eligible' for processing Protected Health Information. The eligible-service list is the boundary.

HDS (Hébergeur de Données de Santé) is the French certification required to host personal health data. It is a France-specific scheme audited by an accredited body — distinct from HIPAA, and increasingly relevant for EU health workloads.

A distinct, named offering that contractually keeps customer data — and ideally operations and support — within the EU/EEA, addressing the gap that ISO/SOC do not cover. Maturity varies enormously: a 'data residency' option is not the same as full operational sovereignty.
Whether the platform hosts Anthropic's Claude family of models.
Whether the platform hosts OpenAI's models — the proprietary GPT and o-series, or only the open-weight gpt-oss.
Whether the platform hosts Google's models — the proprietary Gemini, or the open-weight Gemma.
Whether the platform hosts Meta's open-weight Llama family.
Whether the platform hosts Mistral AI's models.
Whether the platform hosts Cohere's command, embedding and rerank models.
Whether the platform hosts Amazon's own Nova and Titan models.
Whether the platform hosts xAI's Grok family.
Whether the platform hosts DeepSeek's models.
Managed fine-tuning or customisation of the platform's foundation models.
Whether you can bring your own open-weight model and serve it on the platform.
A managed retrieval-augmented-generation service — knowledge bases, vector retrieval, grounding.
A managed runtime for building and orchestrating AI agents.
A managed guardrail layer — content moderation, prompt-injection defence, PII filtering.
Built-in tooling to evaluate and compare model or application quality.
Pay-per-token, on-demand inference with no infrastructure to manage.
Reserved, dedicated inference capacity for predictable throughput.
An OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, usable with the standard OpenAI SDKs.
The top-level isolated network container — the boundary every subnet, route table and gateway lives inside.
The address-range subdivision of the network that workloads actually attach to.
Control over where traffic goes — the routing rules applied to a subnet's egress.
Whether the network can run IPv6, and on what terms.
Connecting two virtual networks directly so they exchange private traffic.
A managed hub that interconnects many networks with transitive routing — the scalable alternative to a mesh of peerings.
An encrypted IPsec tunnel from the cloud network to an on-premises site.
A physical private link into the cloud, bypassing the public internet.
The stateful, per-resource virtual firewall enforced close to the workload.
A stateless allow/deny list enforced at the subnet boundary — the AWS Network ACL model.
A higher-layer managed firewall service — IDS/IPS, deep packet inspection, FQDN filtering.
Defence against volumetric and protocol denial-of-service attacks.
Logging of network traffic metadata for visibility, audit and forensics.
Distributing traffic across backends — at L4 (transport) and L7 (application).
Letting resources in a private subnet reach the internet outbound, without accepting inbound connections.
Reaching a managed or third-party service over a private address, without traversing the internet — the PrivateLink pattern.
Internal DNS zones resolvable only inside the network.
Data leaving the cloud for the public internet — the headline cost line, and the charge that dominates most cloud networking bills.
Data moving between Availability Zones inside one region — the running cost of a multi-AZ, highly-available architecture.
Data transfer from one of the provider's regions to another — replication, multi-region failover and cross-region backups.
The per-gigabyte surcharge for traffic routed through a managed NAT gateway — separate from, and on top of, the gateway's hourly charge.

Outbound data over a dedicated private link — AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute or Google Cloud Interconnect — the route to your own datacentre or another cloud that sidesteps full internet-egress rates.
data sent to the public internet
A central inventory of services, components and their ownership/metadata.
Software templates that create new components, repos or resources on a paved road.
Markdown docs kept beside the code and rendered inside the portal.
Automated standards and maturity checks scored against catalog entities.
How the portal is extended — a plugin runtime, an integration framework, or apps.
Prebuilt connectors to cloud, CI/CD, SCM, observability and incident tools.
Authentication options and role-based access control / permissions.
How the portal runs — self-hosted, managed SaaS, or both. Descriptive, not scored.
Open-source or proprietary. Descriptive, not scored.
The shape of pricing, not the figures. Descriptive, not scored.
Where quotas live + how to raise
The regional vCPU/core quota a fresh standard paid account starts with for general-purpose on-demand instances.
The separate (or shared) quota for spot, preemptible or interruptible capacity.
How many function executions can run at once before throttling, out of the box.
The execution-time ceiling a function can be configured to — the limit you cannot raise.
How many isolated virtual networks one account/subscription/project/tenancy gets per region.
The default allotment of routable IPv4 addresses you can hold per region.
How many managed NAT gateways you can stand up, and against what unit the limit counts.
How many buckets (or the nearest equivalent unit) one account can create by default.
The ceiling on roles, role assignments or service accounts — the quota that bites IaC at scale.
How many managed clusters one account/subscription/project/tenancy can run.
The console surface and CLI for seeing your real values and requesting more — the row to bookmark.
The frequently-accessed default tier: lowest latency, highest storage price, no retrieval fee or minimum duration.
Cheaper storage for data read occasionally — still online and instant, but with a per-GB retrieval fee and a ~30-day minimum.
A colder online tier kept for the rare read: lower storage price, higher retrieval fee, longer minimum — but still no restore wait. Not every cloud offers a distinct instant-cold tier.
The coldest tier: the lowest storage price on the page, paid for with the longest minimum duration, a retrieval fee, and (almost everywhere) a restore measured in hours.
The dimension that decides whether 'archive' fits your recovery plan: is the coldest data online, or behind a restore job that takes hours?
What you pay per gigabyte to read cold data back — separate from, and on top of, any internet egress.
Delete or overwrite an object before this window and you are billed for the remaining days anyway — the penalty that punishes churny archives.
The shorter early-deletion window on the warm-but-cheaper tier — the one most workloads actually use.
The charge to send retrieved data out to the internet — distinct from the storage retrieval fee, and often the bigger number. This is where OVHcloud broke ranks.
The per-operation charge that quietly dominates the bill for small-object, high-throughput workloads.
API gateway, proxy or load balancer?
Three things you put in front of services — and they are often layered, not either/or.
Google Cloud's PaaS-vs-IaaS choice — ship code, or run the machine.
Amazon's two managed relational databases — distributed architecture, or the lower floor cost.
App Service, Container Apps or a VM?
Azure's modern compute choice — the successor to 'web role vs worker role vs VM'.
Three operating models for the same problem: where you sit on the build-vs-buy spectrum.
Cloud Run or App Engine Flexible?
Two ways to run containers on Google Cloud — and Google's own recommended default.
Serverless containers, or containers on instances you run yourself.
NAT gateway, NAT instance or no NAT?
How private-subnet workloads reach the internet — or avoid needing to.
Amazon API Gateway's two API types — the cheaper default, and what still needs the original.
A US hyperscaler's 'sovereign' region gives you operational sovereignty; only an EU-jurisdiction provider gives legal sovereignty — and the CLOUD Act is the reason.
